planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; unlike most clump-forming garden ferns, Creeping Shield Fern spreads steadily by rhizomes to form a true, low, weaving groundcover.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and mulch to keep the shallow rhizomes cool and moist. Creeping Shield Fern, native to Australia and New Zealand, is genuinely rhizomatous and creeping rather than clump-forming like most garden ferns, sending finely divided, soft-textured, lacy fronds up at intervals along spreading underground stems to knit together a continuous low groundcover in the shaded border, a distinct growth habit from the upright, tufted ferns more commonly grown. It tolerates a wide range of shade, from bright dappled light to fairly deep shade beneath trees or shrubs, and spreads at a moderate, manageable pace that fills bare ground without becoming aggressive. Water regularly during dry spells, since consistent moisture keeps the fronds lush and prevents scorching, and divide congested patches in spring if a tidier edge is wanted.

common_name: Forked Felt Fern (Dry-Shade-Tolerant Arrow-Leaved Felted Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Forked Felt Fern bears simple, arrow-shaped, felted fronds rather than the lacy, dissected fronds of most garden ferns, and is notably tolerant of dry shade once established.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in partial to full shade; unlike most ferns, Forked Felt Fern tolerates and even prefers soil that dries between waterings, making it a valuable choice for dry shade under trees where few other ferns will thrive. Its fronds are simple and undivided rather than lacy, arrow- or hand-shaped and covered in a soft, silvery-tan felt of star-shaped hairs that gives the plant an unusual, almost succulent texture and helps it withstand drought, spreading slowly by creeping rhizomes to form a low mat or spilling attractively over rock edges and pot rims. It is easy to grow once sited correctly, needing little more than occasional water during extended dry spells, and works well in a woodland rock garden, on a shaded stone wall, or in a shallow container.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in moderate to dappled shade; King Fern is an ancient, extremely slow-growing fern from the primitive Osmundaceae family that eventually develops a short, woody, trunk-like base over many decades.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in moderate to dappled shade, and provide shelter from drying wind. King Fern is one of the most ancient fern lineages still in cultivation, a member of the primitive Osmundaceae family native to South Africa and Australasia, forming a dense, upright crown of broad, leathery, deep-green fronds around a short, thick, woody base that thickens into a true trunk over many decades of extremely slow growth, eventually becoming a substantial, long-lived specimen prized in mild-climate gardens and conservatories. It demands steady moisture and appreciates humidity, struggling in hot, dry, or exposed sites, but rewards patient gardeners with a striking architectural presence unmatched by faster-growing ferns. Mulch well and avoid letting the root zone dry out, particularly while the plant is young and establishing.

common_name: Bear's Foot Fern (Silvery Creeping-Rhizome Epiphytic Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in loose, well-drained, humus-rich mix in dappled to full shade; Bear's Foot Fern is a rhizomatous epiphytic fern whose furry, silvery rhizomes creep visibly over the surface of the pot or mount, distinct from the upright clump-forming habit of most garden ferns.

directions: Grow in a loose, well-drained, humus-rich mix in dappled light to full shade, mounted on bark, grown in a shallow pot, or tucked into a shaded rock crevice, since Bear's Foot Fern is naturally epiphytic and resents heavy, soggy soil. Its most distinctive feature is a thick, creeping rhizome densely covered in silvery-white, fur-like scales that crawls visibly over the surface of the growing medium and cascades attractively over the rim of a pot or basket, resembling a small furry paw, from which finely divided, glossy triangular fronds arise at intervals. It tolerates full shade well and is notably tough and forgiving for a fern, needing only moderate, consistent moisture rather than constant wetness. Where winters are too cold for outdoor culture, grow it as a container plant that can be moved under cover.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Formosan Wood Fern unfurls new fronds in a striking bright chartreuse-yellow that matures to deep green, and is notably tolerant of dry shade once established.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Formosan Wood Fern, native to Taiwan, unfurls its finely divided fronds in a striking bright chartreuse-yellow each spring, a vivid color unmatched by other Dryopteris in cultivation, before the fronds mature to a rich, glossy deep green for the rest of the season, creating an eye-catching two-tone effect in the shaded border as new growth continues to emerge through the year. It forms a tidy, slowly spreading clump and, once established, tolerates drier shade conditions better than many wood ferns, making it useful under established trees where soil moisture is inconsistent. Remove tattered old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges to keep the clump looking fresh.

common_name: Chilean Hard Fern (Large Bronze-Emerging Colony-Forming Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade; Chilean Hard Fern is a large, colony-forming South American species with thick, leathery, crinkle-edged fronds that emerge bronze-orange before maturing to deep green.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade, and give it room, since this is one of the largest and boldest of the hardy Blechnum ferns. Chilean Hard Fern spreads by creeping rhizomes to form substantial colonies of thick, leathery, ladder-like fronds with distinctively crinkled margins, the new growth emerging a striking bronze-orange before maturing to deep glossy green, creating dramatic textural and color contrast in the shaded border or woodland edge. Its much larger scale and colonizing habit set it apart from the smaller, tighter clumps formed by Deer Fern and other Blechnum species already common in cultivation. Keep soil consistently moist, since it does not tolerate drought, and mulch generously to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature through summer heat.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting 2-3 inches deep with growing tip up; Giant White Wakerobin is a West Coast species bearing cream-white, sometimes pink-blushed flowers held tight against mottled leaves. Never dig from the wild.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2 to 3 inches deep with the growing tip pointed upward; established plants take several years to settle in but persist for decades once happy. Giant White Wakerobin, a West Coast species ranging from California to Washington, bears an unstalked (sessile) flower of cream-white petals, sometimes blushed pink with age, held erect and tight against a whorl of handsomely mottled gray-green and maroon leaves, a larger and often more richly marked plant than the familiar Eastern Trillium grandiflorum. Never dig plants from the wild, since trilliums take five to seven years to bloom from seed and wild populations are vulnerable to overcollection; purchase only nursery-propagated stock. It naturalizes slowly beneath deciduous trees alongside ferns and other woodland wildflowers.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting 2-3 inches deep with growing tip up; Giant Purple Wakerobin bears leaves dramatically marbled purple and silver with deep red flowers. Never dig from the wild.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2 to 3 inches deep with the growing tip pointed upward. Giant Purple Wakerobin, native to redwood and Douglas-fir forests of coastal Oregon and northern California, is grown as much for its dramatically marbled foliage as for its flowers, the broad leaves patterned in bold silver, gray-green, and purple-bronze mottling beneath an erect, deep maroon-red, sessile flower, among the showiest-foliaged trilliums in cultivation. Never dig plants from the wild, since trilliums take five to seven years to bloom from seed and wild populations are vulnerable to overcollection; purchase only nursery-propagated stock. It establishes slowly but rewards patience with a long-lived, increasingly showy woodland colony.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting 2-3 inches deep with growing tip up; Kamchatka Trillium is an East Asian species (Japan, Korea, China, Russian Far East) bearing pure white, three-petaled flowers above a whorl of broad green leaves. Never dig from the wild.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2 to 3 inches deep with the growing tip pointed upward. Kamchatka Trillium is widely distributed across the cool moist forests of Japan, Korea, northeastern China, and the Russian Far East, geographically and taxonomically distinct from the familiar North American trillium species, bearing a broad, pure-white, three-petaled flower above a whorl of three deep-green leaves in early to mid spring, closely resembling and closely related to the beloved Trillium grandiflorum of eastern North America. Never dig plants from the wild, since trilliums take five to seven years to bloom from seed and wild populations are vulnerable to overcollection; purchase only nursery-propagated stock. It naturalizes slowly under deciduous trees alongside ferns and other spring woodland wildflowers.
